title: Plan or Retrieve First? A Scale Study of Tool Discovery Architectures
gist: Apple researchers compare Retrieve-then-Plan with Plan-then-Retrieve for tool discovery by LLM agents on ToolBench (46,984 API endpoints) and find a complexity-dependent crossover: RtP wins on single-tool queries, PtR wins on multi-tool queries. PtR roughly doubles inference cost, motivating complexity-adaptive routing driven by RtP's top-1 retrieval score.

insights.claim: Tool-augmented LLM agents must discover relevant APIs from large registries before planning, because finite context windows prohibit injecting all tool definitions into one prompt.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Tool selection at registry scale is a structural bottleneck for agent platforms.
insights.quote: finite context windows prohibit injecting all tool definitions into a single prompt

insights.claim: The dominant approach, Retrieve-then-Plan (RtP), embeds the user query and retrieves similar tools via approximate nearest-neighbor search.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Embedding-based retrieval is the incumbent; vector search vendors benefit from this default.

insights.claim: Plan-then-Retrieve (PtR) has the LLM first generate Abstract Tool Stubs, hypothesized function signatures describing needed capabilities, and uses those stubs as retrieval queries against the registry.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Moving an LLM call ahead of retrieval changes the cost and accuracy profile of agent stacks.

insights.claim: RtP outperforms PtR on single-tool queries while PtR outperforms RtP on multi-tool queries, a clear complexity-dependent crossover.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Neither architecture dominates; the right choice depends on query complexity.
insights.quote: we find a clear complexity-dependent crossover: RtP outperforms PtR on single-tool queries while PtR outperforms RtP on multi-tool queries

insights.claim: The crossover holds at every retrieval budget from k=1 to 20, across registry sizes from 1k to 47k APIs, and across model families Gemini 2.5 Flash and gpt-oss-120b.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Robustness across scale and models suggests the effect is structural, not model-specific.
insights.quote: robust across registry sizes from 1k to 47k APIs

insights.claim: The study evaluates on ToolBench, with 46,984 unique API endpoints in 50 categories, split into single-tool (G1), intra-category multi-tool (G2) and cross-category multi-tool (G3) query subsets.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Benchmark scale and splits define how far the findings generalize.

insights.claim: PtR exhibits a stub-hallucination failure mode in which the LLM invents plausible but non-existent API names.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Hallucinated names can mislead retrieval, so guardrails matter in PtR pipelines.
insights.quote: the LLM invents plausible but non-existent API names

insights.claim: Stub hallucination cuts both ways: on simple queries PtR's stubs abstract away proper-noun signals that RtP matches directly, while on complex queries the same mechanism decomposes multi-faceted intent into functional sub-needs.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: A flaw can be a feature; the same behavior explains PtR losing on simple queries and winning on complex ones.

insights.claim: PtR's extra discovery call roughly doubles inference cost, which pays off on multi-tool queries but hurts on single-tool ones.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Doubling cost makes always-on PtR uneconomic; spend only where complexity justifies it.
insights.quote: PtR’s extra discovery call roughly doubles inference cost

insights.claim: Complexity-adaptive routing between RtP and PtR is a practical direction, and can be driven by a zero-cost signal already in the pipeline: RtP's top-1 retrieval score.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: A free routing signal lets agent builders capture PtR's accuracy on hard queries without paying its cost everywhere.
insights.quote: a zero-cost signal already present in the pipeline (RtP’s top-1 retrieval score)
